workedExamples.title: Interpreting slope and predicting safely: ŷ = 4x + 20

steps.prompt: A coach tracks practice hours (x) and free throws made out of 100 (y) for players who practiced between 1 and 8 hours. The line of best fit is ŷ = 4x + 20. What does the slope 4 tell you?
steps.reveal: The slope is the change in ŷ for each 1-unit increase in x. So for each extra hour of practice, the model predicts about 4 more free throws made. Slope = rise over run = change in y per 1 unit of x.

steps.prompt: Predict the free throws made for a player who practices 5 hours. Is 5 inside the data range of 1 to 8?
steps.reveal: Yes, 5 is between 1 and 8, so this is interpolation — reliable. Substitute x = 5: ŷ = 4(5) + 20 = 20 + 20 = 40. The model predicts 40 free throws made.

steps.prompt: Now a player claims they will practice 30 hours, so the model predicts ŷ = 4(30) + 20 = 140 made. What is wrong with trusting that number?
steps.reveal: Two things. First, 30 is far outside the data range of 1 to 8 — that is extrapolation, and the linear trend may not hold out there (the trap: extrapolates-blindly). Second, 140 free throws out of 100 is impossible, which is a clue the line was never meant to stretch that far. Plugging numbers in is easy; trusting predictions outside the observed range is the mistake.

steps.prompt: State the safe rule for using a line of best fit to predict.
steps.reveal: Predict only for x-values inside (or very near) the range where data was actually collected. Inside the range the relationship was observed and the prediction is trustworthy; far outside it, you are guessing that the pattern continues — which it may not.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting the y-intercept in context: when x = 0 makes sense, and when it does not

steps.prompt: A line of best fit for cars aged 1 to 10 years is ŷ = −1500x + 22000, where x = age in years and y = resale value in dollars. What does the intercept 22000 represent?
steps.reveal: The intercept is the value of ŷ when x = 0. Here x = 0 means a brand-new car (zero years old), and 22000 dollars is a sensible price for a new car. Because x = 0 is meaningful and sits right at the edge of the data range, the intercept can be read as the predicted value of a brand-new car.

steps.prompt: Now a different study fits ŷ = 2x − 100, where x = a student's height in centimeters (data from 150 to 190 cm) and y = a test score. What does the intercept −100 mean?
steps.reveal: Literally it is the predicted score when x = 0 — a student 0 cm tall. That is impossible and far outside the data range of 150 to 190 cm. So the intercept −100 has NO real-world meaning here; it is just where the line happens to cross the axis. Reading it as a real score is the trap: intercept-interpreted-out-of-context.

steps.prompt: What is the difference between the two intercepts above?
steps.reveal: In the car example, x = 0 is real (a new car) and near the data, so the intercept is a meaningful prediction. In the height example, x = 0 is impossible and far from the data (150–190 cm), so the intercept is meaningless in context. Always ask: does x = 0 make real-world sense, and is it in or near the data?

steps.prompt: State the rule for interpreting an intercept.
steps.reveal: Interpret the y-intercept as a real-world value only when x = 0 is meaningful AND inside or near the data range. Otherwise the intercept is just a mathematical anchor for the line, not a fact about the world.
